name: Task-Set Inertia
summary: The tendency of the mental configuration you used for the previous task to keep running and get in the way of the next one, which is one cause of switch costs.
explanation:
A task set is the mental configuration a task needs: which stimuli you pay attention to, which rules you apply and which responses you give. Task-set inertia means that this configuration does not switch off when you change tasks. It keeps running for a while, and it gets in the way of the new task.

Alan Allport, Elizabeth Styles and Shulan Hsieh proposed the idea in 1994 to explain a puzzle in task-switching experiments. Even when people get plenty of time to prepare for a switch, they are still slower and make more errors on the first trial of the new task. That residual switch cost suggests that part of the cost comes from the old task, which is still active. Preparing for the new task does not cover all of it. A related observation is the asymmetric switch cost: switching back to an easy, dominant task can cost more than switching to a hard one. Why? The dominant task had to be strongly suppressed, and that suppression lingers.

Think of task-set inertia as the lab-level, millisecond-scale version of attention residue, which describes the same effect at the scale of real work. Both say the previous task does not leave the stage when you tell it to. So what can you do about it? Group similar work so that consecutive tasks share a task set (task batching). Leave a short buffer between very different kinds of work, and expect the first minutes after a switch to be slower and more error-prone.
